lesson.title: Reaction Time Kinematics Lab
lesson.buzzAssessmentTitle: Unit 1 Lesson 4: Reaction Time Kinematics Lab Analysis

assessmentSettings.feedbackPolicy: Show concise process feedback after submission. Use this metadata and the Essay a. lines for BusyBee grading.

requiredCopiedValues: Level 1 trial reaction times and ruler drops
Level 2 trial reaction times and finish gaps
Level 3 trial reaction times and finish gaps

humanReviewTriggers: Student cites reaction times outside the plausible human range (under 0.1 s or over 1 s) with an explanation that could still be valid.
Student gives a partially correct explanation that does not fit the rubric cleanly.
Student uses different valid vocabulary or method than the model answer.
Student answer is blank, copied from the prompt, or too vague to verify.
Student cites trial values that contradict their stated conclusion.

questions.objective: Compare a measured reaction time to average-human and elite benchmarks
questions.prompt: Calculate your fastest Level 1 reaction time from your smallest recorded ruler drop. Was it closer to the average human visual reaction time (about 0.25 s) or to an elite athlete's reaction time (about 0.15 s)? Cite the drop you used and the time you calculated.
questions.requiredEvidence: The smallest recorded ruler drop and the reaction time the student calculated from it. The simulator shows only the drop distance; it never displays reaction times.

criteria: States their smallest recorded ruler drop and the reaction time they calculated from it.
Compares the calculated time numerically to both the 0.25 s average and 0.15 s elite benchmarks.
States which benchmark it is closer to, consistent with the cited value.
Gives a plausible calculated time and picks a benchmark but does not cite the drop it came from.
Compares to only one benchmark.
Cites values but the closeness judgment is weakly explained.
Gives no calculated value.
Gives an impossible value (under 0.1 s or over 1 s) with no explanation.
Makes no comparison to either benchmark.

commonMisconceptions: Reporting the ruler drop distance in cm as if it were the reaction time in seconds.
Assuming a faster-than-elite time means great reflexes rather than a lucky guess or anticipation.

feedback.fullCredit: Strong work. Your comparison uses a time you calculated from your own data.
feedback.partialCredit: Revise by citing your smallest recorded drop and the reaction time you calculated from it, then compare that time to both the 0.25 s and 0.15 s benchmarks.
feedback.noCredit: Run Level 1 again, note your smallest ruler drop, calculate the reaction time it corresponds to, and compare that number to 0.25 s and 0.15 s.
feedback.teacherNote: Flag for review if the cited time is implausible but the reasoning is otherwise sound.

questions.objective: Explain why a reaction-time head start grows during constant acceleration
questions.prompt: In a constant-speed race, a reaction-time head start stays the same distance for the whole race. In your Level 2 drag races, the head start grew into a much larger gap by the finish line, even though both cars accelerate at exactly the same rate. Explain why, citing the two reaction times from one of your races and the finish gap you calculated from them.
questions.requiredEvidence: Both reaction times from at least one Level 2 race and the finish gap the student calculated from them. The simulator shows both reaction times; it never displays the gap.

criteria: Cites both reaction times from one of their races and the finish gap they calculated from them.
Explains that the car that launched first is always moving faster than the trailing car at every moment during acceleration.
Concludes that the distance between the cars therefore keeps growing until the finish, unlike the fixed gap in a constant-speed race.
Says the gap grows because the cars are speeding up but cites no values from their own races.
Cites their reaction times but does not explain why the leader is always moving faster than the trailer.
Claims the gap stays the same during the race.
Attributes the gap to different accelerations or different top speeds.
Gives no usable explanation.

commonMisconceptions: Believing equal accelerations must produce an unchanging gap.
Thinking the winning car accelerated harder instead of simply launching earlier.

feedback.fullCredit: Good reasoning. The leader's head start means it is always moving faster at each moment, so the gap keeps growing.
feedback.partialCredit: Add the two reaction times from one of your races and the finish gap you calculated from them, and explain what the leading car's speed is doing compared to the trailing car's speed at the same moment.
feedback.noCredit: Rerun Level 2, record both reaction times, calculate the finish gap from them, and compare the two cars' speeds at any instant: which car is always moving faster, and why?
feedback.teacherNote: Accept equivalent explanations phrased as the trailing car repeating the leader's earlier, slower speeds.

questions.objective: Compare visual and auditory reaction times using measured data
questions.prompt: Levels 1 and 2 used visual signals (a released ruler, a green light). Level 3 used a sound (the starter gun). Were your visual and auditory reaction times different? Use example values from your trials: your Level 2 reaction time is shown in the readouts, and your Level 1 and Level 3 reaction times are the ones you calculated.
questions.requiredEvidence: At least one visual reaction time (shown in Level 2, or calculated from a Level 1 drop) and one auditory reaction time (calculated from a Level 3 finish gap and opponent RT).

criteria: Cites at least one visual reaction time from Level 1 or 2.
Cites at least one auditory reaction time from Level 3.
States whether the times differ and by roughly how much, with a conclusion consistent with the cited values.
Makes a correct comparison but cites values from only one signal type.
Cites values from both signal types without stating a conclusion.
Cites no trial values.
The stated conclusion contradicts the values given.

commonMisconceptions: Assuming visual reactions must be faster because light travels faster than sound, ignoring how the brain processes each signal.
Comparing a Level 2 gap distance (m) against a Level 3 reaction time (s) as if they were the same quantity.

feedback.fullCredit: Well supported. Your conclusion follows from your own visual and auditory measurements.
feedback.partialCredit: Add a specific reaction time from the missing signal type so the comparison uses both kinds of data.
feedback.noCredit: Get one visual reaction time (your Level 2 readout, or calculate one from a Level 1 drop) and one auditory reaction time (calculate it from a Level 3 finish gap and opponent RT), then say which was faster for you.
feedback.teacherNote: Either conclusion (visual faster or auditory faster) is acceptable when the cited data supports it.

questions.objective: Connect the 0.100 s false-start rule to the limits of human reaction
questions.prompt: In Level 3, reacting in less than 0.100 s counts as a false start, just like in real track events. Why are Olympic sprinters disqualified for reacting in less than 0.100 s, and what does that rule show about human limits?
questions.requiredEvidence: Reference to the 0.100 s threshold and what a faster start implies.

criteria: Explains that roughly 0.1 s is the minimum time for a human to hear the gun, process the signal, and start moving.
Concludes that a faster start must be anticipation or guessing rather than a true reaction.
Connects the rule to a biological limit on nerve-signal and muscle-activation time.
Says a faster start means the sprinter guessed or jumped early but does not connect it to signal-processing time.
Describes the human limit but never ties it back to why the rule exists.
Says faster reactions are simply better.
Treats 0.100 s as an arbitrary rule with no physical meaning.
Gives no explanation.

commonMisconceptions: Believing elite athletes can genuinely react in under 0.1 s with enough training.
Thinking the rule punishes fast reflexes instead of detecting anticipation.

feedback.fullCredit: Exactly right. Under 0.1 s the start happened before the signal could be processed, so it must be a guess.
feedback.partialCredit: Add why 0.1 s matters physically: how long does it take the sound to be heard, processed, and turned into muscle movement?
feedback.noCredit: Try to false-start in Level 3 and read the disqualification message, then explain what a sub-0.100 s start really means.
feedback.teacherNote: Flag for review if the student argues from personal Level 3 data in an unusual but plausible way.
